questions.question: Describe the main instruments of protection and explain why protection is described as a transfer from consumers to producers.
questions.expected_answer: Tariffs are customs duties that raise an import's shelf price so home products compete more easily, yielding state revenue. Quotas cap import quantities and hand valuable licences to favoured firms, which is why economists dislike them more than tariffs. Producer subsidies lower domestic costs, hiding the protection in the budget rather than at the border. Exchange control rations foreign currency so importers cannot pay abroad. Administrative barriers include import bans, zealously applied standards and deliberate red tape; export incentives mirror these on the selling side. Dumping is selling exports below cost or below home price, often to eliminate rivals, answered by WTO-sanctioned anti-dumping duties (applied by South Africa on some chicken portions and steel); an infant industry is a promising new industry that could match foreign costs once grown, the classic candidate for temporary shelter. Every instrument raises prices or narrows choice for domestic consumers, transferring welfare from millions of consumers — each losing a little — to concentrated producers and workers who each gain a lot; this thin-spread-loss, concentrated-gain asymmetry makes protection politically easy and economically expensive.

questions.question: Evaluate the arguments for protection against the case for free trade, and compare import substitution and export promotion as development strategies with reference to South Africa.
questions.expected_answer: For protection: infant industries need shelter until scale lowers costs (rebuttal: infants rarely admit to growing up, and permanent shelter breeds inefficiency); protection saves jobs (rebuttal: visible jobs are saved at the cost of invisible ones downstream, plus retaliation); anti-dumping defence against predatory pricing (the strongest card, accepted even by free traders); diversification and strategic self-sufficiency; balance-of-payments and revenue support. For free trade: comparative advantage raises total output; consumers gain lower prices and choice; competition disciplines domestic monopolies; world-scale markets open; technology travels with trade. The desirable mix is broadly open trade with targeted, temporary, conditional protection under sunset clauses. Import substitution replaces imports with home production behind tariff walls: industry starts and imports fall, but firms stay small (capped by the home market) and inefficient, as in apartheid-era South Africa. Export promotion helps firms sell to the world through incentives, infrastructure and finance: no market ceiling, efficiency forced by global competition, as in East Asia — but it collides with WTO subsidy rules and requires working logistics. Democratic South Africa chose the outward path — tariff cuts, IPAP and sector master plans, with automotive incentives the flagship and poultry, clothing and steel the contested protected cases — while ports, rail and electricity constraints throttle export performance.

questions.question: Explain globalisation and the role of the WTO, and describe the four forms of economic integration with African examples.
questions.expected_answer: Globalisation is the accelerating integration of national economies — goods, services, capital, technology, information and people crossing borders at unprecedented volume and speed — driven by container shipping, telecommunications and the internet, financial liberalisation, and successive trade agreements. The line runs from the GATT of 1947 through eight tariff-cutting rounds to the Uruguay Round, which created the WTO in 1995. The WTO's rules: most-favoured-nation non-discrimination (a benefit granted to one member extends to all), national treatment of imports once inside a border, bound tariffs, and dispute settlement so members litigate rather than retaliate. Critiques: rich countries still protect agriculture, where developing countries hold advantage; the rules constrain industrial policies rich countries themselves once used; and gains are unevenly shared. Integration ladder: a free trade area abolishes tariffs among members who keep their own external tariffs — the AfCFTA, the world's largest by membership, aiming to give African industry a market of over a billion people; a customs union adds a common external tariff — SACU (South Africa, Botswana, Namibia, Lesotho, Eswatini), the world's oldest, sharing revenue by formula; a common market adds free movement of labour and capital; an economic union adds harmonised policies and possibly a single currency — the EU with the euro. South Africa participates at several rungs: SACU, the SADC free trade area and the AfCFTA.
